name: Uzbekistan
snapshot: A Taliban-built canal set to divert up to a fifth of the Amu Darya's flow threatens Uzbekistan's cotton and wheat fields, testing Mirziyoyev's engagement with Kabul.
culture: Samarkand, Bukhara and Khiva were great cities of the Silk Road, and their blue-tiled madrasas and mausoleums draw growing numbers of tourists. Plov, rice cooked with meat and carrots, is a national ritual. The Uzbek suzani embroidery and Margilan silk are prized crafts.
society: Central Asia's most populous country has opened up since 2016, ending forced child labour in cotton fields, freeing the currency and attracting investment. But politics remains tightly controlled, and Mirziyoyev extended his rule through a 2023 constitution. The Aral Sea, drained by Soviet irrigation, is an environmental disaster.

story: The Aral Sea was once the world's fourth-largest lake. Then Soviet planners diverted the rivers that fed it, chiefly the Amu Darya, to grow cotton in Uzbekistan's desert, and within a few decades most of it was gone, leaving rusting fishing boats on salt flats and dust storms full of pesticide residue. Uzbekistan's 2026 was a reminder that the region's water fights are not over. They are getting worse.

The new threat comes from upstream. Taliban-ruled Afghanistan is building the Qosh Tepa canal, about 285 kilometres long, to turn northern desert into farmland using Amu Darya water. Construction of its second phase was under way in 2026, with operation provisionally set for 2028, and estimates suggest it could cut the river's flow by 15 to 20 percent, water that Uzbek and Turkmen farms depend on (Times of Central Asia). Afghanistan has no water-sharing agreement with its neighbours. President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, who once warned the canal could "radically change" Central Asia's water balance, has chosen engagement over confrontation: in April he proposed a regional decade of water action, and on 9 October he called for regular, structured water talks with the Taliban (Afghanistan International). Uzbekistan also won a UN resolution naming the Aral Sea region a zone of environmental innovation. For a country of 37 million whose farms and cities live on two rivers, this is an existential question that does not make headlines.
briefing.power: A presidential republic with a dominant executive. A 2023 constitution extended presidential terms to seven years and reset Mirziyoyev's term count, allowing him to stay until 2037. Parliament has two chambers; all parties support the president and there is no real opposition.
briefing.holders: President Shavkat Mirziyoyev, in office since 2016.
